concepts.query:
Content Discovery

We exported every page on the site into a spreadsheet and audited the collection: who owns each page, when it was last updated, what type of content it is and which topics it covers. Reading a sample closely showed what the content actually means, how it is structured and how well each section serves its purpose, before any redesign began.

Contextual Research

Before redesigning the portal, we studied the conditions around it rather than the content itself: the organization's reporting lines, its procurement rules, the technical limits of the platform it runs on and the market of competing services. That contextual research explained why earlier redesigns had stalled and which constraints any new structure had to respect.

Competitive Review

For the credit union's redesign, we reviewed six competitors' websites against criteria that mattered to the organization: how clearly each explained fees, how easily members could find rates and how each handled online applications. The competitive review showed where the credit union stood and what its members had come to expect from similar services.

Heuristic Analysis

Without recruiting any participants, I reviewed the existing checkout flow against established usability heuristics: visibility of system status, consistency, error prevention, and recognition rather than recall. The heuristic analysis noted where the site followed or departed from each one, rated each problem's severity and gave the team a ranked list to fix before testing with users.

Process Mapping

We followed a grant application from submission to payment, documenting every step, system and handoff. The process map showed applications waiting days in a shared inbox, data rekeyed between two systems and a review step nobody owned. Diagramming the business process exposed those inefficiencies, and showed where better content and tools would actually help.

Stakeholder Engagement

We started by identifying everyone with an interest in the redesign and asking what they needed from it and what they could contribute. Throughout the project we kept those stakeholders informed and involved in decisions, shared work in progress for critique, and addressed concerns early, before a disagreement about the navigation could become an obstacle.

User Research

To understand the people the archive serves, we spent time with researchers, students and staff, observing how they look for records, asking about their goals and frustrations, and watching them complete real tasks. That user research revealed needs and motivations no analytics dashboard showed, including how often people search for a person rather than a document.

Contextual Inquiry

Rather than asking warehouse staff how they used the inventory system, we observed them at work during a busy shift, watching where they looked things up and what notes they kept beside the screen. Direct observation in their real environment surfaced workarounds nobody had mentioned in interviews, and countered the recall bias that self-reported behavior carries.

Mental Models

From interviews and a card sort, we synthesized how patients think about their care: not in terms of departments, but as a journey from symptoms to appointment to follow-up. We captured that mental model as diagram and two short narratives, giving the team a shared picture of users' frames to design the navigation and labels around.

User Interviews

We held twelve one-to-one interviews with small business owners, asking how they think about payroll, which tools they prefer and how they handled their last tax filing, as they recall it. Each interview ended with a short interactive task on the current site. The conversations surfaced vocabulary and priorities we later used to label the new sections.

Best Practices

Rather than invent a navigation pattern for the new intranet, we started from conventions proven across many sites: a persistent global menu, breadcrumbs and a predictable footer. We reviewed the established guidance for forms and labels, judged our early designs against it, and departed from a best practice only where research showed our users' situation was genuinely different.

Collaborative Design

The new patient portal was designed in collaborative working sessions with clinicians, schedulers, patients and the developers who would build it. Each group sketched, critiqued and chose between options together, so decisions drew on their combined knowledge. Because everyone had a hand in shaping the design, the team shared a commitment to it long after the workshops ended.

Design Principles

Before sketching, the team agreed on five design principles specific to the library's audience, such as "plain words over catalog terms" and "every page says what to do next." When two options competed, we tested each against the principles, which kept our decisions consistent and easy to explain, and gave us criteria for evaluating the finished design.

Systems Thinking

A category added for one campaign quietly broke navigation another team relied on, and the cleanup came months later. A systems thinking approach treats the site, its content and the people who maintain it as one system of interacting parts and processes, watching how changes influence each other over time, including the delayed and nonlinear effects no single team would predict.

Semantic Web

We published the museum's collection with its meaning made explicit: each artwork, artist and place has a URI and is described with shared, formally defined vocabularies. Other institutions' data can now be integrated with ours, software can reason over the combined graph to infer connections no single catalog records, and the same ontology forms a semantic layer over internal systems.

Knowledge Graphs

For a food bank, we modeled distribution sites, neighborhoods and services as entities with typed relationships: a site serves a neighborhood and offers fresh produce. Integrating schedules from several sources into one knowledge graph, software can query the connected data and infer answers no source states directly, such as which nearby sites are open today.

Linked Data

Each event page on the site now includes JSON-LD describing the event with schema.org: its name, dates, venue, performers and ticket offers, with links to the venue's and performers' own identifiers. Search engines read that linked data to show event details directly in results, and partner calendars import it without anyone copying listings by hand.

Information Architecture

When people can't find information on a site, the cause is usually structural. Information architecture work organizes, structures and labels the content of a shared information space: how it is classified, what each category is called and how people move through it. Each part is designed and tested so users can find what they need and complete their tasks, and the structure holds as content grows.

Navigation Design

We redesigned how people move through the university site. A simpler navigation model puts five audience-based entry points in the main menu, breadcrumbs show where people are, and contextual links on each page point to where they can go next. Secondary navigation allows them to move easily within explicitly defined sections. Clear signposts at every level mean a visitor arriving from a search engine can still find their way around.

Search

The search logs showed which queries returned zero results. We added synonyms so abbreviations and old product names match current terms, tuned relevance ranking so title and topic matches outrank body text, and rebuilt the results page with filters and autocomplete. Known-item searches now land on the first page of results, and exploratory searches can be refined instead of abandoned.

Taxonomy

We turned a drifting tag list into a controlled vocabulary: a preferred label, alternate labels and a definition for each concept, arranged in a shallow hierarchy so editors classify content consistently. Stored as a standards compliant SKOS taxonomy, each tag references a managed concept that drives filters, retrieval and related content, and a regular review keeps the taxonomy effective as new subjects appear.

User Experience Design

We designed the whole experience of renewing a professional license, not just the form: the reminder email, the explanation of requirements, the payment step and the confirmation that follows. Research with license holders guided how content, tools and interactions were coordinated across each stage, so the renewal felt like one service rather than a string of separate pages.

Interaction Design

We specified how the booking form responds to every action: which choices become available after a date is picked, what feedback appears when a time slot is full, and how the interface moves between its loading, error and confirmation states. Each response was designed to be predictable and coherent, so people always knew what had happened and what to do next.

Automation

Tagging two thousand legacy articles by hand wasn't practical, so we automated it: a script runs each night, classifies new and changed articles against the vocabulary, validates required fields and flags anything below a confidence threshold for an editor. The repeatable work now runs on a schedule with little human intervention, and people handle only the exceptions.

Python

I wrote a Python script to analyze the article archive: it loads every document, uses an NLP library to extract keywords and entities, and writes the results to a CSV for review. Python's readable syntax and large ecosystem of libraries made the analysis quick to build, and the script runs from the command line whenever the archive changes.

Javascript

The product page works without JavaScript, then progressively enhances: a small script adds an image zoom and live stock updates in the browser. The account area is a React single-page application, and the same JavaScript validation code runs on the server under Node.js, so each form rule is written once and enforced in both places.

Technology Integration

The newsroom adopted a language model to draft summaries, but only after integrating it into the existing publishing workflow: the CMS sends each new article to the service, stores the draft summary in its own field and routes it to an editor for review. Connected this way, the tool exchanges data with existing systems instead of becoming one more product to manage.

Evaluation

Once the new structure was built, we evaluated whether it achieved what it was designed to do. We tested key tasks with people, inspected pages against accessibility and content criteria, and measured how long pages took to load and how often searches succeeded. The results showed which goals the design met and where it needed another round of work.

Performance Evaluation

We measured how quickly the news site delivered content on a mid-range phone over a slow connection. The performance evaluation found nearly three megabytes of scripts and images on the home page, much of it never used, and a web font that blocked rendering. After trimming the payload, the first article loaded in under two seconds, even on less capable devices.

Usability Testing

Five representative users attempted realistic tasks with a clickable prototype while we observed and they thought aloud. We noted where each one succeeded, struggled or failed: labels they misread, paths they abandoned, answers they didn't recognize. The team fixed the biggest design problems and tested the revised prototype again with a new round of participants.

Accessibility Evaluation

We assessed whether people using assistive technologies could use the registration site: navigating every form by keyboard alone, listening to each page with a screen reader, checking color contrast for low vision and testing reduced-motion settings. The accessibility evaluation found unlabeled form fields and a focus trap in the date picker, and checked each fix against WCAG.

Content Modeling

For a museum, we modeled exhibitions, artworks, artists and events as separate content types. Each type has its own attributes, such as an artwork's medium and year, and the relationships between types (an artist made an artwork, an exhibition includes it) link one page to the next. Managed as structured data in the CMS, the content model lets the same content be delivered to the website, a kiosk and partner channels.

Content Strategy

The college had thousands of pages and no plan. Our content strategy started from established goals for enrollment and student support, then decided what content each audience needed, in what form and from which team. We set a publishing plan, assigned owners and defined the governance that keeps content accurate, so the site could be sustained after relaunch.

Prototyping

We built a working prototype of the new knowledge base into the platform within two weeks: a few real content types, a hundred migrated articles and a rough front end. Testing it with staff showed which parts of the content model held up, and building it exposed a constraint in the platform's search that no diagram would have revealed before full production.

Sanity

In Sanity Studio I defined schema types for articles and authors, customized the desk structure, added a custom input and a document action that checks required fields, and installed several plugins built by the Sanity community. A GROQ query pulls each article with its author and topics from the Content Lake, and a webhook rebuilds the site whenever an editor publishes.

Card Sorting

Thirty participants sorted cards labeled with the site's main topics into groups that made sense to them, then named each group. The card sort revealed how people expect the information to be grouped and labeled: most put billing and payments together, and almost nobody used the internal term the organization had built its navigation around.

Tree Testing

Before building the new navigation, we ran a tree test: participants saw only a text hierarchy of labels and were asked where they would look for items like "replace a lost card" and "update an address." Success rates and the paths people took showed which labels matched their expectations and which parts of the proposed structure sent them the wrong way.

Domain Modeling

Working with subject matter experts, we mapped the key concepts in a city's permitting domain (permits, projects, properties, inspections and the people involved) and the relationships between them. That domain model gave us a structured representation of how the subject itself is organized, so the later content model and navigation could rest on it rather than on the org chart.

User Interface Design

We redesigned the dashboard's visual hierarchy so the most important figures stand out: a clear typographic scale, restrained color, consistent controls and generous spacing. The layout adapts from a wide desktop grid to a single column on phones, and every element comes from a shared library of interface components, so the visible surface stays consistent across screens.

Site Maps

The site map for the redesign showed every page type and section as boxes in a hierarchy, with lines for the main navigational paths between them. We used the diagram to plan the structure with the team and review it with stakeholders, while noting its limit: for a collection that grows weekly, it shows where pages sit, not the rules that decide where new ones go.

Content Operations

To run content as an ongoing function rather than a launch project, the team mapped the workflows by which articles are produced, reviewed, published and retired, named an owner for each step and set policies for review dates. We also designed the team's technology solution to work with their content operation, as opposed to against it. Governance meetings now approve changes to the content model and the vocabulary, so the structures behind the content stay current at scale.

Web Writing

We rewrote the service pages for how people read on screens: they scan, search and often arrive in the middle of a task. Headings now state what each section answers, sentences are short, and one term is used consistently for each idea. A brief style guide set the voice, tone and terminology so every writer on the team produces clear, concise copy.

Discovery

Before proposing changes to the agency's site, we spent three weeks in discovery: inventorying what the site holds, interviewing the people who use it and why, reviewing the systems and budget it depends on, and learning what it costs to maintain. That understanding of the product and the conditions around it shaped every recommendation that followed.

Structural Analysis

We assessed how the product catalog was built: the content types in the CMS, the attributes each one is composed of and the relationships linking products, parts and manuals. The structural analysis found fields used inconsistently, relationships stored as plain text and types that duplicated each other, so the new model could keep what worked and fix what didn't.

Human Centered Design

We grounded every decision for the benefits application in the needs, abilities and contexts of the people applying: many on phones, some using screen readers, most short on time. They took part throughout, through interviews, early prototypes and repeated rounds of evaluation, so the design followed their goals rather than the agency's internal structure.

Goals

At the kickoff we worked with leadership to define three goals for the redesign: raise online applications by a fifth, cut calls about application status in half and make every service page accessible. Each goal had a measure and a target. When later requests competed for time, we traced each one back to those agreed goals to decide what made the scope.

Use Cases

Before writing requirements, we documented the use cases the new portal had to support: a parent registering a child for school, a teacher updating a class roster, an administrator exporting attendance. Each described who was acting, what they were trying to accomplish and in what circumstances, so scope and priorities rested on concrete needs rather than a feature list.

Natural Language Processing

To find recurring themes in five years of support tickets, we used natural language processing: the text was cleaned and tokenized, keywords and named entities were extracted, and tickets were clustered by similarity using embeddings. Turning that unstructured text into data showed which problems came up most, and which tickets described the same issue in different words.

Standards Compliance

We rebuilt the site to conform to published standards: valid, semantic HTML, WCAG accessibility criteria, schema.org metadata and a SKOS vocabulary for topics. Validators run on every build to test conformance. Working to shared specifications means the site behaves predictably across browsers and assistive technologies, and its data stays usable as the tools around it change.

Programming Languages

The project used three programming languages, each for what it does best: JavaScript for the interactive front end, Python for the scripts that clean and analyze content data, and SPARQL for querying the knowledge graph. Each has its own syntax and rules for expressing what a computer should do, and choosing the right one for each task kept the code simple.

SPARQL

A SPARQL query against the museum's triple store finds every artwork by artists born in a given city, following relationships from artwork to artist to birthplace across the graph. A second query pulls in data from a public endpoint and combines both sources in one result, and an update query corrects a mistyped date across hundreds of records at once.

Engineering Products

Rather than build a content repository, a search service and a deployment pipeline from scratch, the team adopted ready-made products for each and spent its time configuring them: content types in the CMS, an index in the hosted search service and build settings on the deployment platform. The engineering effort went into connecting those systems, not writing them.

CMS

The team moved its content into a headless CMS: authors work in an editing interface with structured fields, the content repository stores each item once, and an API delivers it to the website, the mobile app and the digital signage. Separating content from presentation means a new channel can be added without changing how authors create and organize content.

Continuous Integration

Every commit to the site's repository triggers a workflow that installs dependencies, builds the site, runs link and accessibility checks, and deploys only if every check passes. The same workflow runs when an editor publishes in the CMS, so content changes go through identical, repeatable steps, and a broken build surfaces within minutes instead of in production.

AI

We tested how well a large language model could summarize policy documents and answer staff questions about them. The assistant produced fluent summaries and handled common questions well, but invented details when a document was ambiguous and struggled to classify edge cases. We kept it for drafting, with an editor checking every answer, and documented its limits for the team.

Graph Databases

We moved the parts catalog's relationships into a graph database: parts, assemblies, suppliers and documents are nodes, and the connections between them are stored directly as relationships. Queries that took several joins in the relational database now follow those relationships in one step, and new kinds of things can be added without reorganizing the data already stored.

Frameworks

Starting the new site from a framework rather than from scratch gave us routing, a component model, a build pipeline and conventions for organizing files on the first day. The team spent its time on content and design instead of rebuilding that foundation, and new developers could find their way around because the framework's structure was already familiar.

RDF

We expressed the manufacturer's product data in RDF: every product, component and supplier has a URI, and each fact is a statement linking a subject to an object through a named relationship. Serialized as Turtle and validated with SHACL shapes, the statements merged cleanly with a partner's data into a single graph that both teams could query together.

Astro

We rebuilt the marketing site in Astro: pages render to static HTML at build time from content in a headless CMS, and only the search box and an image carousel ship client-side JavaScript, as interactive islands. A few preview routes run on the server so editors can see drafts on request. Pages load fast because almost nothing runs in the browser.

Design Outcomes

Six months after the redesign, we judged it by how well the site served its audience: whether visitors could find the right service, understand what it required and complete it without calling the help desk. Those design outcomes, measured through task success and support volume, came from decisions about structure, labeling, interactions and the relationships between pages.

Interoperability

The state's health departments each kept facility data in different systems. By agreeing on a shared schema and exchanging records through a common API, each department's data can now be accessed and used by the others' systems and by public services, without manual reformatting. Interoperable data made a statewide facility finder possible, and keeps it current.

Content Reuse

Each medication's safety warning is written once and stored as its own piece of content. The same warning appears on the drug's page, in the printable patient handout, in the mobile app and in a partner's formulary, published as is or shortened for small screens. When the warning changes, every channel updates without anyone rewriting or duplicating it.

Discoverability

Visitors couldn't find the foundation's research reports, even though they were on the site. We improved discoverability by organizing the reports by topic and audience, labeling them with the terms people actually use and connecting each report to related programs and news. People now find and understand what the reports offer, because the structure matches what they expect.

Engineering Outcomes

We judged the migration by what software could do with the result: content stored in an open format, every item with a stable identifier, data exchanged through a documented API and a schema that downstream systems could validate against. Those engineering outcomes came from implementation choices about formats, schemas and infrastructure, not from anything visible on the page.

Machine Readability

We made the clinic's opening hours, services and locations machine readable: each is entered as typed, structured data instead of a paragraph of prose, and published with explicit markup. Search engines, voice assistants and booking agents can now interpret and act on that information directly, answering "which clinic is open now" without a person reading the page.

Structured Content

Rather than writing finished pages, the team broke each procedure into discrete, meaningful pieces: its steps, warnings, the device it applies to and its audience. That structured content is consistent and predictable enough for both people and machines to understand, so the same pieces are reused across the website, an app and a printed guide, and an update made once appears on every platform.
